t.1.173.1: Arjuna said: For what reason did King Kalmāṣapāda appoint his own wife to the guru, the best among the knowers of Brahman?
t.1.173.2: Why did that great-souled Vasiṣṭha, who knew the highest dharma that wins the worlds, go in to a woman who should not be approached? You should tell me, who am asking, all that he did long ago.
t.1.173.4: I have already told you before, O best of the Bharatas, how that king was cursed by the great-souled Śakti, the son of Vasiṣṭha.
t.1.173.3: Dhanaṃjaya, hear this which you ask of me about the invincible Vasiṣṭha, and likewise about the king who overpowers his enemies.
t.1.173.5: But the king, scorcher of foes, having fallen under the power of the curse, his eyes troubled with anger, went forth from the city together with his wife.
t.1.173.6: Having gone with his wife to a deserted forest, crowded with herds of many kinds of deer and teeming with creatures of every sort, he wandered about there.
t.1.173.7: Seized by the curse, he wandered through the forest, which was covered with many kinds of shrubs and creepers, surrounded by many kinds of trees, and filled with terrible sounds.
t.1.173.8: Once, seized by hunger and searching for food for himself, he, sorely distressed, saw at a certain forest waterfall a brāhmaṇa woman and a brāhmaṇa who had come together for lovemaking.
t.1.173.10: Seeing her husband seized, the brāhmaṇī then spoke: "Hear my words, O king, which I shall speak to you, O you of good vows."
t.1.173.9: Seeing the two of them running away in terror, their desire unfulfilled, the king seized the brahmin by force as they fled.
t.1.173.11: For you, sprung from the lineage of Āditya, are renowned throughout the world; vigilant, you stand firm in dharma and delight in obedient service to your elders.
t.1.173.12: You have received a curse, O invincible one; you ought not to commit a sin. Now that my season has come, I was to have been united with my husband today.
t.1.173.14: While she was thus crying out, that doer of exceedingly cruel deeds devoured her husband, as a tiger devours a coveted deer.
t.1.173.13: For my purpose with my husband is not yet fulfilled, and great is my longing for offspring. Be gracious, best of kings; let this husband of mine be set free.
t.1.173.15: The tear that fell to the ground from her, overcome with anger, became a blazing fire, and it set that region ablaze.
t.1.173.16: Then that Brahmin woman, burning with grief and anguished by the calamity that had befallen her husband, cursed the royal sage Kalmāṣapāda in her wrath.
t.1.173.17: Because you, vile one, like a cruel brute, have today devoured my lord, my greatly renowned husband, while I looked on with my purpose still unfulfilled,
t.1.173.18: Therefore you too, O evil-minded one, wounded by my curse, shall give up your life the very moment you approach your wife in her season.
t.1.173.19: And the seer Vasiṣṭha, whose sons were destroyed by you, will unite with your wife, and she will bear a son. That son of yours will carry on your lineage, O vilest of kings!
t.1.173.20: Having thus cursed the king, that lovely Āṅgirasī entered the blazing fire in his very presence.
t.1.173.21: And the illustrious Vasiṣṭha saw all this through his great yoga of knowledge and through his austerity, O scorcher of foes.
t.1.173.22: Then, after a long time, the royal seer was freed from the curse; when he approached her in her fertile season, he was held back by Madayantī.
t.1.173.23: For the king, bewildered by the curse, did not remember that curse. Then that best of kings, having heard the words of the queen and recalling that curse, was sorely tormented.
t.1.173.24: For this reason, O best of the Bharatas, the king, burdened with the taint of the curse, appointed Vasiṣṭha to his own wife.
